pr_body:
It's possible that an anomaly detection job can output a flurry
of quantiles documents for use in renormalization in the time that
a single renormalization takes.

When this happens we only use the most recent quantiles document
for the next renormalization, but the previous code queued up all
the quantiles documents until the next renormalization started.

The new approach that this PR implements is to only keep the most
recent new quantiles document while the current renormalization is
in progress. This avoids wasting memory on a queue that will be
largely discarded (apart from one element) later on.

Fixes #85539
pr_title: [ML] Avoid multiple queued quantiles documents in renormalizer

review_comment:
This means that `renormalize` will not accept new requests until `waitUntilIdle` returns. If thats cool, then alright.

Previously, `waitUntilIdle` didn't block `renormalize`. It simply waited until all work was done and no new work was added.

Ah, yes, it's only for a tiny fraction of a second, but it could happen.

It's like we need a mechanism to ask if we could acquire the semaphore without actually acquiring it.

> It's like we need a mechanism to ask if we could acquire the semaphore without actually acquiring it.

OK, there is an `availablePermits()` method that does this, but the problem is that then we'd be doing a busy wait instead of waiting for a wakeup from the OS.

We need something other than a `Semaphore`.  Maybe a `Phaser` or `CyclicBarrier`.  I will have another go at it.

Now this means that if the currently running renormalization fails, those quantiles are gone. I suppose this is ok as we are only ever wanting the latest. But will we skip forward in time and miss the earliest part of the window?

Ah, 
```
new AugmentedQuantiles(quantiles, latestQuantilesHolder.getEvictedTimestamp(), latestQuantilesHolder.getLatch());
```
We keep track of it to ensure we renormalize far enough back. Nice.

actually, reading back, this code doesn't seem to have ever done what it was supposed to because the queue would have been empty because of `getLatestQuantilesWithLatchAndClear`. 

The only time the queue wouldn't be empty is if `renormalize` was called again. Then a new set of quantiles would be added. We would still miss that failed renormalization window as the old requests are all gone.

The only way to capture the failed renormalization window is to somehow remember the failed timestamp as `getLatestAugmentedQuantilesAndClear` clears it out and its lost forever. Which, i suppose is ok :/

I've preserved the old functionality:

- It doesn't remember the earliest time if a renormalization fails
- It does remember the earliest time if we discard a quantiles document because we got a newer one before the earlier one was processed

Failed renormalizations should be rare so I don't think this will make a difference very often. I'd rather just make the one change in this PR. If there is a user who repeatedly gets failed renormalizations then I don't want to introduce another build-up of work by remembering the earliest time forever.

EDIT: Below was my previous comment, but thinking about it more, I think the loop is still required as we want to allow new normalizes to come in and be executed. We want to make sure all normalization is idle, including handling the case when new ones coming after the current thread stops executing.

------- my old comment for context --------

Does this still need to be in a `do {} while(latch != null)` loop? It seems that the `phaser` is doing the required work here by waiting for the executing thread to finish. 

If the latch is not null that means:
 - We wait for the latch to finish (current quantiles)
 - Wait for the `doRenormalizations` to finish, which may do more than one as `latestQuantilesHolder` can be updated
 - Executor thread completes (meaning all passed quantiles are finished)
 - We go back through the loop again (which isn't synchronized, so another `normalize` call could happen)
 - See the new latch (or maybe not?)
 - go through it again

> We want to make sure all normalization is idle, including handling the case when new ones coming after the current thread stops executing.

Yes, that's it.
